content: 1. Pregnant women in low HIV-burden settings who have unknown or HIV-negative status and are in serodiscordant relationships, whose partners do not have suppressed viral loads on antiretroviral therapy (ART), or who have other known ongoing HIV risks should be retested during late pregnancy, ideally at a third-trimester visit. If the initial test or retest is missed or delayed, catch-up testing should be conducted. 2. An additional HIV retest in the postpartum period may be considered for women with unknown or HIV-negative status who belong to key populations or have partners with HIV who do not have suppressed viral loads. Countries may also consider implementing postpartum testing in specific districts or provinces. 3. Priority populations for HIV testing include those most affected by HIV with high ongoing risk, those critical to achieving and sustaining low HIV incidence, and those with specific individual or structural vulnerabilities related to HIV. These populations often include men, adolescents, young people, pregnant women, infants, children, serodiscordant couples, sexual and drug-injecting partners of people living with HIV, migrants, refugees, displaced populations, and other vulnerable groups. 4. For infants and children, nucleic acid testing (NAT) at birth can be added to existing early infant diagnosis approaches to identify HIV infection among HIV-exposed infants. This is a conditional recommendation based on low-certainty evidence. 5. In high HIV-burden settings, infants and children with unknown HIV status who are admitted for inpatient care or attending malnutrition clinics should be routinely tested for HIV. This is a strong recommendation with low-certainty evidence. 6. In high HIV-burden settings, infants and children with unknown HIV status should be offered HIV testing in outpatient or immunization clinics. This is a conditional recommendation based on low-certainty evidence. 7. Point-of-care nucleic acid testing should be used to diagnose HIV in infants and children younger than 18 months. This is a strong recommendation with high-certainty evidence. 8. Rapid diagnostic tests for HIV serology can be used to assess HIV exposure among infants younger than four months. For infants and children aged 4–18 months, HIV exposure status should be determined through serological testing of the mother. This is a conditional recommendation with low-certainty evidence. 9. Rapid diagnostic tests for HIV serology can be used to diagnose HIV infection in children older than 18 months, following the national testing strategy. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence. 10. An indeterminate range of viral copy equivalents should be used to improve the accuracy of all nucleic acid-based early infant diagnosis assays. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence. 11. National regulatory agencies are encouraged to adopt point-of-care early infant diagnosis without unnecessary delays, using streamlined registration and approval processes for immediate implementation. 12. Biological children of parents living with HIV (or who may have died of HIV) should be routinely offered HIV testing services. If found to be infected or at high risk of infection through breastfeeding, they should be linked to treatment or prevention services and offered a broader package of voluntary provider-assisted referral. 13. HIV testing services should be routinely offered to all key populations in both community and facility-based settings. Community-based HIV testing, with linkage to prevention, treatment, and care, should complement facility-based testing for key populations in all settings. This is a strong recommendation with low-certainty evidence. 14. Social network-based approaches can be offered as an HIV testing strategy for key populations as part of a comprehensive package of care and prevention. This is a conditional recommendation with very low-certainty evidence. 15. Adolescents from key populations should be offered HIV testing services with linkage to prevention, treatment, and care. This is a strong recommendation with very low-certainty evidence. 16. Adolescents should receive counseling on the potential benefits and risks of disclosing their HIV-positive status and be supported in deciding whether, when, how, and to whom to disclose. This is a conditional recommendation with very low-certainty evidence. 17. In high HIV-burden settings, HIV testing services with linkage to prevention, treatment, and care are recommended for all adolescents. This is a strong recommendation with very low-certainty evidence. 18. In low HIV-burden settings, HIV testing services with linkage to prevention, treatment, and care should be accessible to adolescents. This is a conditional recommendation with very low-certainty evidence. 19. Governments should revisit age-of-consent policies to uphold adolescents' rights to make decisions about their health and well-being, considering their maturity and understanding. 20. All pregnant women should be tested for HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) at least once and as early as possible during pregnancy. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence for syphilis and low-certainty evidence for HBsAg, particularly in settings with ≥2% HBsAg seroprevalence in the general population. 21. Dual HIV and syphilis rapid diagnostic tests can be used as the first test in HIV testing strategies and algorithms in antenatal care. 22. Provider-assisted referral should be offered to all people with HIV as part of a voluntary comprehensive package of testing and care. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence. 23. Couples and partners should be offered voluntary HIV testing services with support for mutual disclosure. This is a strong recommendation with low-certainty evidence. 24. Women who disclose any form of violence by an intimate partner or sexual assault by any perpetrator should be offered immediate support. Health-care providers should, at a minimum, offer first-line support when women disclose violence. If unable to provide first-line support, providers should ensure someone else is immediately available to do so. This is a strong recommendation based on indirect evidence. 25. Health-care providers should inquire about exposure to intimate partner violence when assessing conditions that may be caused or complicated by such violence to improve diagnosis, identification, and subsequent care. This is a strong recommendation based on indirect evidence. 26. Mandatory or coercive HIV testing is never warranted. Providers should assess the risk of harm and the most appropriate approach for couple and partner testing, including supportive options such as provider assistance, and identify situations where couple or partner testing is inadvisable. 27. Post-test counseling and services should be implemented as part of an explicit linkage strategy to guide individuals to appropriate care. The core package of post-test services includes clear counseling messages, referral and rapid ART initiation, and additional links to HIV prevention, care, support, and other relevant services. 28. HIV testing services should be integrated with other relevant clinical services, such as those for tuberculosis, viral hepatitis, sexually transmitted infections, maternal and child health, sexual and reproductive health, and harm-reduction programs for people who inject drugs. Integration aims to make HIV testing more convenient and increase uptake. 29. Decentralization of HIV testing services involves providing testing at peripheral health facilities and in community settings. This approach can reduce transport costs and waiting times, increasing uptake, especially among men, young people, and key populations. 30. Task sharing involves redistributing tasks from highly trained health-care providers to those with shorter training, such as lay providers and peer workers, to address workforce shortages. Trained lay providers can deliver all aspects of HIV testing services, including pre-test information, performing rapid diagnostic tests, interpreting results, post-test counseling, and linking individuals to prevention, treatment, and care services.
